summary: Describes a framework for IPFIX Mediation, defining Mediator components that sit between exporters and collectors of IP flow data. It extends the reference model of RFC 5470 and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IPFIX exports records about network flows to collectors. RFC 6183 describes a mediator that can convert, select, aggregate, anonymize, or correlate records before sending them onward.

questions: what are intermediate processes in ipfix
how do ipfix mediators handle tls
what are the five ipfix intermediate processes
subtitle: A framework for processing IPFIX flow records between exporters and collectors.

tldr.problem: A direct IPFIX exporter-to-collector design may not scale well or provide the processing flexibility measurement applications need.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an IPFIX Mediator that receives record streams, applies one or more Intermediate Processes, and exports the transformed records.
tldr.outcome: The document extends the IPFIX reference model with mediation functions and security guidance. It is Informational and updates RFC 5470.

today: RFC 6183 is Informational and was published in April 2011. It updates RFC 5470 and describes a framework rather than new IPFIX messages.

sections.title: Why Add a Mediator
sections.content:
The IPFIX model in RFC 5470 has exporters send flow information to collectors. The RFC says this direct design may face scalability problems and may not offer enough flexibility for different measurement applications.

An intermediate entity can process flow records or packet reports before a collector receives them. It can also convert non-IPFIX records into IPFIX or change the IPFIX transport, such as converting from UDP to SCTP to improve export reliability.
sections.plainLanguage: A mediator sits between IPFIX sources and collectors. It can process records or convert them before forwarding them.

sections.title: Mediators and Intermediate Processes
sections.content:
IPFIX Mediation is the manipulation or conversion of a record stream for later export using IPFIX. An IPFIX Mediator receives records, hosts one or more Intermediate Processes, and exports the resulting stream as IPFIX messages.

An Intermediate Process transforms a record stream using record contents, state kept across records, or other data. It may receive input from a collector, a metering process, a file reader, another Intermediate Process, or another source. Its output can go to an Exporting Process, a file writer, or another process.
sections.plainLanguage: A mediator receives a stream of records, applies processing, and exports the result. Intermediate Processes perform the individual transformations.

sections.title: The Mediation Reference Model
sections.content:
A mediator can receive IPFIX Flow Records, PSAMP Packet Reports, or records from non-IPFIX sources. It can send the processed output to one or more collectors or to other mediators, so mediators can be chained.

A typical mediator has one or more Collecting Processes, Intermediate Processes, and Exporting Processes. Mediation can also run inside an Original Exporter between metering and exporting, or alongside IPFIX file readers and writers. The framework does not assume how record streams reach a mediator.
sections.plainLanguage: A mediator can receive records from several kinds of source and send results to collectors or other mediators. Processing can also be placed inside an exporter or around stored files.

sections.title: Five Processing Functions
sections.content:
The RFC names five Intermediate Process types. Conversion maps non-IPFIX records or changes transport; Selection passes records that match a value or range; Aggregation merges records spatially or over time; Anonymization deletes or changes fields; Correlation combines records or metadata to derive information.

Processes may run in parallel on copies of the stream or in sequence, where one process feeds the next. Aggregation and correlation may cache records and need expiration rules. When the data layout changes, the flow-key indicator must reflect the resulting fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The five named processes translate, filter, combine, anonymize, or correlate records. They can be arranged in sequence or run on separate copies of the data.

sections.title: Preserving Trust Across a Mediator
sections.content:
A mediator terminates one transport session and starts another, so TLS does not provide a single end-to-end session between the Original Exporter and the downstream collector. The RFC says a mediator should generally maintain the same integrity and confidentiality protection on both sides.

By default, data received over TLS or DTLS should be sent onward over TLS or DTLS. A mediator must not imply that unprotected source data is trustworthy merely by protecting the outgoing connection, and it should tell the collector when original protection was absent. Records from multiple sources must remain separate unless the mediator is explicitly combining them.
sections.plainLanguage: A mediator creates separate security connections on its two sides. It should not weaken protection or make untrusted input appear trustworthy.
